video_title: Why Wall Street Still Can’t Fully Use Ethereum
gist: Mo Jalil (ex-Goldman Sachs algo trading, ex-Ethereum Foundation APAC BD) and Oscar Thorin (ex-Status, early PSE member) discuss ETH Systems, a for-profit privacy-and-institutions spinout from the Ethereum Foundation launched roughly a month before recording. They argue institutional privacy — not scaling or research — is now the binding constraint on Wall Street using public Ethereum, describe unsolved multi-billion-dollar use cases like interdealer trade compression and four-party regulated payments, and predict a wave of venture-scale institutional privacy businesses within 24 months as regulatory clarity converts long-running bank innovation projects into real procurement.

themes.theme: Privacy as the binding constraint on institutional Ethereum

insights.claim: Institutions optimize for two things — their business and being compliant — which pushes them toward environments they control (private/permissioned chains), and only cryptography lets them keep those properties while accessing public Ethereum's deep liquidity.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Frames privacy tooling as the gating factor determining whether institutional volume lands on public Ethereum L1/L2s or on walled-garden bank chains — a direct fork in the road for ETH's fee and settlement accrual.
insights.quote: But you can't get both without cryptography.

insights.claim: Demand for privacy from institutions is now massive and in some circumstances exceeds demand for privacy from individuals, a reversal driven by the last few years of regulatory clarity.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Suggests the monetizable privacy market is B2B/institutional rather than retail-anon, redirecting where privacy protocol value likely accrues.
insights.quote: there's a massive massive demand for privacy of institutions. Um and I think that's come about sort of with the last few years uh sort of where there's been more regulatory clarity

insights.claim: Institutional Ethereum adoption is now largely an engineering problem rather than a cryptography research problem, though specific institutional constraints still force customization beyond off-the-shelf privacy rollups.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil and Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Implies capital should flow to integration/productization teams rather than to new base-layer cryptography research for this market segment.
insights.quote: I think at least for the kind of use cases that we look at, it's I think largely more of an engineering problem as opposed to like a research problem.

insights.claim: Privacy is only one of several properties institutions require; security, censorship resistance, scalability and formal technical specifications must all be satisfied simultaneously before a firm already running billions through a working system will migrate to Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Explains why partial solutions stall in procurement and why migration timelines are longer than crypto-native teams assume.

insights.claim: Institutional buyers span an extreme sophistication spectrum, from firms with 20-person in-house R&D departments staffed with cryptography PhDs to firms that simply want a white-label solution.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Signals room for two distinct business models — deep co-development for tier-one desks and packaged white-label products for the long tail.

insights.claim: Interdealer trade compression — where banks hand all trades and positions to a trusted third party to net them out — costs individual banks millions to hundreds of millions of dollars per year, and a shared confidential state on Ethereum could disintermediate that third party entirely.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete, quantified rent being extracted by an incumbent intermediary that ZK-enabled shared state could attack — a several-billion-dollar addressable market few crypto teams are looking at.
insights.quote: they pay millions of dollars a year, by the way, tens of millions, if not hundreds of millions of dollars a year

insights.claim: The interdealer compression opportunity is essentially unrecognized in crypto, with most teams the speaker has talked to never having seen the business or the problem, despite it being a several-billion-dollar market.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: A whitespace flag: early teams building confidential netting infrastructure face little crypto-native competition.
insights.quote: this in itself is a several billion-dollar basically business that could be kind of taken a look at

insights.claim: A jurisdiction attempting nation-scale confidential payments requires four parties on every transaction — sender, receiver, order taker and the government — rather than the standard two, and spent years failing to find any existing protocol that met the TPS and computational-cost requirements, publishing a 16-page report on why it was impossible.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Shows the real blocker for sovereign-scale on-chain payments is multi-party regulatory structure plus throughput, not payment privacy per se — a spec requirement worth watching in payment-protocol roadmaps.
insights.quote: they have a regulatory requirement to have four actors for payments. This is the sender, the receiver, the order taker, and then the government

insights.claim: Well-known use cases like private payments and tokenized deposits are already effectively solved for some organizations in some countries; the remaining hard work is jurisdiction-specific permutations of those use cases.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Reframes competitive positioning: generic private-payments startups face commoditization, while jurisdiction-specific compliance engineering carries the margin.

insights.claim: Private RFQs are cited as an example of an already-proven venture-scale institutional privacy business, with Zama pointed to as a recent entrant operating at a scale few others were.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Concrete comparable for pricing the institutional confidential-trading category and identifying which private-market names sit in it.
insights.quote: For example, private RFQs, right? I think Zama did something recently where I personally think that's a huge business

insights.claim: Failing to serve institutional privacy needs on Ethereum does not remove the demand — those institutions instead shelve the project or move to a private network.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Frames public-chain privacy tooling as directly competitive with permissioned enterprise chains for the same settlement flow.
insights.quote: Or worse yet, gone to I say worse yet, gone to some kind of private network.

themes.theme: Demand signal and the institutional clock

insights.claim: Over the next 24 months a wave of new venture-scale institutional privacy businesses will emerge, timed off the fact that a typical institutional engagement takes at least 18 months end to end.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable forecast: deals signed now surface as revenue-generating products by roughly mid-2028, setting the window for early positioning in this category.
insights.quote: I'll make a prediction over the next 24 months you're going to see a whole number of businesses pop up that are like that

insights.claim: The institutional sales cycle decomposes into several months to reach and educate the buyer, several more months of procurement, and roughly a year to ship an initial version.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for revenue timing at any crypto company selling to banks — announced pilots should be discounted by this lag.

insights.claim: Demand is overwhelmingly inbound rather than sold, with almost no outbound selling required to bring institutions to Ethereum privacy work.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Inbound-led demand is the strongest early evidence of genuine product-market fit for institutional on-chain infrastructure.
insights.quote: most of the demand has been inbound

insights.claim: Regulatory clarity including the GENIUS Act flipped institutional posture last year from exploratory innovation-team proofs of concept to CEOs directing teams to do real business.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Marks a regime change from budget-line experimentation to P&L-owned deployment — the leading indicator for real institutional volume on chain.
insights.quote: a CEO would basically pick up the phone talk to the innovation team and be like, "Hey, look, you guys have been working on this for 5 years. Uh we actually want to do business now."

insights.claim: Traditional asset managers are approaching every week or two asking how to put their products on chain, driven by watching DeFi rather than by pitches.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: A frequency datapoint on tokenized-product pipeline that precedes public announcements by 12-18 months.
insights.quote: I have this conversation almost every single I would say week or two. Like people are saying, "Hey, how do we do this?"

insights.claim: What institutions actually want is 'institutional DeFi' — the affordances of Aave, Uniswap and Lido delivered in a compliant, confidential form — and DeFi protocols are already producing forked versions of their products to serve it.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Points to permissioned/compliant forks of blue-chip DeFi as the vehicle for institutional flow — relevant to how value accrues (or leaks) from the original protocol tokens.
insights.quote: the things like Aave and Uniswap and Lido, they want those things, but they want to do it in a way that they're compliant

themes.theme: The nonprofit ceiling and the for-profit spinout

insights.claim: Institutional conversations at the Ethereum Foundation repeatedly died at the point where the institution asked how to pay, because the Foundation had to stay neutral and refuse — a structural limit that motivated spinning out a for-profit entity.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Evidence that unmonetized institutional demand had been accumulating inside the EF, and a template other foundation teams may follow into commercial spinouts.

insights.claim: Large institutions frequently cannot transact with nonprofits at all — being a nonprofit is treated as a procurement red flag — so a for-profit vehicle is required to do the last mile of institutional delivery.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Non-obvious structural constraint: nonprofit-led crypto ecosystems will systematically under-capture institutional revenue without commercial arms.
insights.quote: being a non-profit is actually a red flag sometimes and they just can't work with you

insights.claim: Public goods funding is described as extremely hard to sustain over a multi-year journey, with the view that grants should be reserved for teams that genuinely need them rather than funding work with an obvious paying customer.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Suggests further migration of capable crypto R&D talent from grant-funded to revenue-funded structures.
insights.quote: public goods funding is extremely extremely hard and in my opinion grants should be given to people that really need it

insights.claim: The operating model runs two coupled workstreams: paid institutional engagements (architecture reviews, POCs, requirement mapping) that generate proprietary business intelligence, which is then generalized and released as open-source building blocks and technical specifications.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: A commercial-to-public-goods flywheel in which institutional budgets end up funding Ethereum ecosystem infrastructure — worth watching as a funding model for other protocol layers.

insights.claim: The strategy is deliberately bespoke first and generalized second — go deep on highly specific institutional use cases, then extract reusable components into a switchable stack — on the view that generic infrastructure built ahead of demand does not get adopted by large institutions.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil and Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Contradicts the dominant crypto pattern of shipping generic infra and waiting for users; a filter for judging which institutional-privacy teams will convert.
insights.quote: And like if you build it, they will come. That's not always the case, especially when you talking about these large institutions with like very specific requirements.

insights.claim: Institutional adoption requires meeting hundred-year-old organizations on their own terms and translating their existing business into on-chain form, because teams that tried to force institutions to adopt crypto-native patterns have failed.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: A diligence heuristic: prefer institutional-crypto teams staffed with people who can speak the incumbent's language over crypto-native teams pushing their own form factor.

insights.claim: Privacy should be defined as who can see what, when, and how — selective disclosure — rather than as hiding, and zero-knowledge proofs allow aggregate metrics like TVL thresholds or trade correctness to remain publicly verifiable while individual accounts and positions stay confidential.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil and Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Resolves the main objection to on-chain privacy for DeFi analytics; the resulting design pattern determines whether on-chain data businesses survive an institutional privacy wave.
insights.quote: I think privacy really is who can see what, when, and how.

insights.claim: Full on-chain transparency actively harms execution quality, illustrated by a $55 million TWAP order on Uniswap mainnet being visibly front-run by observers, and by traders' entire histories being readable on Hyperliquid — a fundamental constraint for institutions.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Execution leakage is the concrete, quantifiable cost that will drive institutional flow toward confidential venues — bearish for fully transparent order flow venues absent a privacy layer.
insights.quote: there's like this Ethereum whale with $55 million T-wopping into like Lit on the main Uniswap layer one, and everyone is like, "Oh, look at this guy." It's like then the price is front-running this individual

insights.claim: Open source and open specifications are a hard requirement for institutional trust in confidential systems, because security-by-obscurity cannot establish the security and privacy properties these buyers must verify.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Argues closed-source enterprise privacy vendors are structurally disadvantaged in this market, favoring permissively licensed protocol stacks.

themes.theme: Ecosystem gaps and the cypherpunk-boardroom bridge

insights.claim: There is a massive disconnect between what institutions are asking for and what the Ethereum ecosystem is building, and closing that feedback loop is described as an unmet ecosystem-wide need rather than a solved coordination problem.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Identifies the requirements-gathering layer as the scarce input; teams with real institutional requirement data hold an information edge over protocol builders guessing at demand.
insights.quote: there's a massive massive disconnect in terms of what the institutions are asking for and so what the ecosystem provides

insights.claim: Publishing open-source privacy work is itself a distribution channel into banks — a large number of banks read the public repository and write-ups, and one sovereign-scale payments prospect found the team through published proof-of-concept work after years of failed internal searches.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Open-source publishing, not sales, is the demonstrated lead-generation mechanism in institutional crypto — a signal to watch which teams' repos institutions actually engage with.
insights.quote: I will tell you right now the number of banks that look at it is pretty large.

insights.claim: Institutional adoption will first build a distinct, siloed, private arena separate from mainstream DeFi, and only later intertwine with core protocols like Morpho and Uniswap — a sequencing the guests confirmed matches their internal view and what sophisticated institutions are already planning for.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman, confirmed by Mo Jalil and Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Implies near-term institutional volume does not immediately lift blue-chip DeFi metrics; the composability integration is the later, larger catalyst to watch.

insights.claim: The team's explicit positioning is 'cypherpunks in the boardroom' — getting into rooms where institutional decisions are made in order to install cypherpunk defaults, on the view that institutional demands like removing counterparties and cypherpunk demands like decentralization are the same requirement in different vocabulary.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil and David Hoffman
insights.so_what: If true, institutional adoption need not dilute Ethereum's core properties — a rebuttal to the thesis that TradFi capture degrades censorship resistance.
insights.quote: the position that we often have is like cypherpunks in the boardroom. Like, that's super counterintuitive because these are the two types of groups that normally don't talk to each other.

insights.claim: Institutions practice jurisdictional and regulatory arbitrage in the same way individuals choose when privacy is worth the cost, meaning their constraints are environmental rather than ideological and can be designed around.
insights.speaker: Oscar Thorin
insights.so_what: Predicts institutional on-chain activity concentrates in whichever jurisdictions offer the desired legal properties — a map for where regulated on-chain venues get domiciled.

insights.claim: In a seven-year horizon the ambitious case is that the vast majority of financial infrastructure runs on a blockchain with privacy invisible to non-crypto-native users, enabling things like trading US stocks from outside the US without revealing identity via a DID system.
insights.speaker: Mo Jalil
insights.so_what: Defines the terminal state being underwritten — global permissionless access to tokenized equities with identity abstraction is the endgame product to track progress against.
insights.quote: Like in 7 years, it's very realistic that the vast majority of financial infrastructure is going to be on a blockchain. It's happening right now. All the biggest players are already doing it.
